title: Cellar and Hymn
premise: Felix Whitlock, a nonbinary property surveyor sent to appraise the derelict Halloway farmhouse, discovers the house responds to being measured—rooms shift, doors multiply, and their own sleep recordings capture a second voice answering questions in Felix's voice. The voice belongs to Wren Halloway, bound into the house since 1911 by a family covenant that trades a member's soul each harvest moon for the land's prosperity. As the harvest moon rises, the current covenant-holders, the Vane family who bought the land, arrive to complete the harvest and intend to use Felix as the replacement vessel. Felix and Wren, falling in love across a century of separation, break the covenant by un-inviting what was invited in—renaming the house itself—destroying the house's power at dawn but freeing Wren into the world, changed and mortal, at Felix's side.
about_author: Petra Nakamura is a former building inspector from coastal Oregon whose decade of surveying condemned properties left her with a folder of houses that 'felt wrong.' She writes horror about the intimacy of old buildings and the contracts we sign without reading.

chapters.title: The Commission
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Felix. A property firm assigns Felix the Halloway farmhouse appraisal—unusual, since the Vane family bought it sight unseen and wants it assessed before the harvest festival. Felix arrives at dusk, notes the house is warm despite no power, and counts eleven doors from outside. The beat is professional unease curdling into curiosity.

chapters.title: Eleven Doors, Ten Rooms
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Inside, Felix counts only ten doors. Retracing steps, the eleventh reappears behind them. Measurements won't hold—the tape reads different lengths each pass. Felix sets up camp in the kitchen, keeps lights on, and begins the survey log that will structure the novel. Beat: rationality asserting itself against a first undeniable wrongness.

chapters.title: What the Walls Answer
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix taps walls to test for hollows; something taps back, in kind, then in rhythm—almost conversation. A child's chalk hopscotch grid appears overnight on the kitchen floor, numbered in a hand decades dead. Felix photographs everything. Beat: the shift from surveyor to witness.

chapters.title: The Recording
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. To monitor sleep-talking during the overnight stay, Felix leaves a recorder running. Playback at dawn: Felix's own voice asking questions—'Are you still there?' 'Do they know?'—and a second voice, low and dry, answering in words the mic barely holds. Beat: terror braided with the first flicker of compassion for the answering voice.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Following the voice to the sealed cellar, Felix finds a name scratched into the doorframe: WREN HALLOWAY, 1911. The recorder, left on the cellar steps, captures a full sentence: 'Don't let them count you in.' Felix researches the Halloway family at the county library. Beat: the house becomes a person with a name.

chapters.title: The Covenant of the Vanes
chapters.summary: Interleaved POV: library archives and a present-day scene of Ambrose Vane preparing for the harvest moon with his family, rehearsing an old litany. The archive reveals the Halloways traded a member each harvest for the farm's prosperity, and the Vanes inherited the covenant with the deed. Beat: the horror acquires an institutional face—duty dressed as tradition.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix begins deliberately recording questions at night. The voice—Wren—answers in fragments: she was nineteen, she was chosen by lot, the house 'keeps' what it's given. Felix realizes Wren can only speak where the house permits. Beat: intimacy forming through a wall, love beginning as attention.

chapters.title: The House Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The house begins evaluating Felix: doors open onto rooms from Felix's own past—a childhood bedroom, a hospital corridor—rendered perfectly and slightly wrong. The house is learning what Felix is worth. Beat: vulnerability; the surveyor realizes they are the surveyed.

chapters.title: Vane's Arrival
chapters.summary: Alternating Felix and Ambrose Vane POVs. The Vanes arrive early, polite and cold, insisting Felix stay through the harvest festival 'for the appraisal.' Ambrose inspects the cellar door with proprietary tenderness. Felix notices the Vane children wear iron bells. Beat: the trap closing with a handshake.

chapters.title: The Litany of the Land
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, eavesdropping. The Vanes perform a rehearsal rite; Ambrose's daughter Miriam, twelve, recites the litany flawlessly and then asks, quietly, who it will be this year. Ambrose says the land will 'choose.' Felix understands the Vanes are also captive. Beat: complicating the enemy—power corrupting its own servants.

chapters.title: Through the Cellar Door
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. During a blackout staged by the house, the cellar door stands open. Felix descends and meets Wren—not a ghost but a presence woven into the house's structure, visible as a girl of nineteen made of dust and lamplight. They speak face to face for the first time. Beat: the love story becomes real, and doomed.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, first time. Wren recounts 1911: her father invited 'the Keeper of the Yield' into the land during famine; it demanded a keeper of its own, and the house grew around her. She explains the covenant's mechanism—the house needs a named keeper before moonrise or it takes one. Beat: the rules of the trap, delivered with a century of grief.

chapters.title: The Appraisal Report
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix tries to warn the Vanes with evidence; Ambrose burns the survey log, revealing he knows exactly what the house is and has fed it before—his wife, years ago, 'lost to the county.' Miriam overhears. Beat: rage and the moral stakes crystallize; Felix cannot walk away.

chapters.title: Miriam's Question
chapters.summary: Miriam Vane's POV. Miriam sneaks to Felix, asking if the house took her mother. Felix tells her the truth. Miriam reveals the litany's hidden verse: the covenant can be broken only by 'un-inviting'—renaming the house in the Keeper's presence before moonrise, which requires a keeper's consent. Beat: hope with a terrible price—Wren must consent to be unmade.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix offers Wren the escape: un-invite her, end the covenant, though it may destroy her rather than free her. Wren, who has been a wall for a hundred years, asks instead what sunrise feels like. Beat: love against duty—Felix refuses to trade Wren's existence for their own safety.

chapters.title: Moonrise
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The harvest moon rises; the house seals itself, doors vanishing, rooms rearranging into a labyrinth. Ambrose begins the harvest rite with Miriam's bells ringing. The house, needing a keeper, begins pulling Felix toward the cellar—Wren screaming through every wall. Beat: full siege; the house turns predator.

chapters.title: The Counting
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Lost in the shifting house, Felix survives by refusing to count—doors, steps, breaths—starving the house of the measurement it feeds on, while Wren's voice guides them through walls that no longer exist. Beat: the surveyor weaponizes their own discipline by breaking it.

chapters.title: Miriam's Bells
chapters.summary: Miriam's POV. Miriam turns on her father, casting down the iron bells and reciting the litany backward, stalling the rite. Ambrose, corrupted past reason, moves to name his own daughter as keeper. Felix reaches the cellar as the moon crests. Beat: the child breaks the chain of duty; the father embodies its corruption.

chapters.title: The Un-Inviting
chapters.summary: Felix and Wren POVs interleaved. In the cellar, before the Keeper's rising pressure, Felix speaks the renaming: 'This house is not yours. You were never invited. Leave.' Wren consents, whispering her own true name into the words. The house convulses; the Keeper is cast out of the land; Wren begins to unravel. Beat: climax—the truth spoken aloud as exorcism.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The house collapses inward, rooms folding shut, and Felix carries Wren—solid now, mortal, gasping, alive—out through the last remaining door as dawn breaks. Ambrose is gone, taken by what he served; Miriam stands free in the field. Beat: cost paid, dawn as literal and emotional release.

chapters.title: The Final Appraisal
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, weeks later. Felix files the report: structure unsound, recommend demolition. Wren, learning to eat and sleep and grieve her century, asks Felix to teach her to measure things—'so I know they'll stay.' Miriam writes once, from an aunt's home, to say thank you. Beat: tender resolution; belonging built rather than inherited.

chapters.title: Cellar and Hymn
chapters.summary: Dual epilogue, Felix and Wren. In Felix's small apartment, Wren hums a hymn her mother sang in 1911, and Felix, recording it, hears only one voice now—hers, warm, answering no one's questions but her own. The last line of the survey log: 'Twelve doors. All of them open.' Beat: quiet coda—love that survived the house, counting nothing, keeping everything.
